title: Count Valid Substrings I
spaceBreakdown:
- int p, int n, int r, long long ans: scalars → O(1)
- no containers, no recursion, no auxiliary arrays
- not counted: input string s
approach: For each ending index r, a substring s[l..r] is invalid exactly when it contains "abc". All such invalid substrings ending at r must start at or before the beginning of the most recent "abc" occurrence that ends at or before r. So we track p = the starting index of the most recent "abc" occurrence (initialized to -1). Whenever s[r-2..r] == "abc", we update p = r-2. Then the number of valid substrings ending at r is r - p (start indices from p+1 to r). Summing over all r gives the answer. This is correct because any "abc" occurrence ending after r doesn't affect substrings ending at r, and p is the tightest left boundary.
hints: For a fixed ending index r, what shape does the set of valid starting indices take? The constraint n ≤ 10^5 rules out checking every substring individually.

Track p = the starting index of the most recent "abc" occurrence ending at or before r (a single sliding pointer). In s = "abc", at r = 2 we detect s[0..2] = "abc" and set p = 0, so valid substrings ending at r = 2 are those starting at indices 1 and 2, contributing r − p = 2.

```
p = -1
ans = 0
for r in 0 .. n-1:
    if r >= 2 and s[r-2..r] == "abc":
        p = r - 2
    ans += r - p
return ans
```

**Smallest input** - only one character, so the loop body runs exactly once.
`Input: s = "a"` → `Expected: 1`
⚠️ Bug: starting the loop at r = 1 instead of r = 0 → returns 0.

**Boundary occurrence** - "abc" ends at the earliest possible index r = 2.
`Input: s = "abc"` → `Expected: 5`
⚠️ Bug: checking `r > 2` instead of `r >= 2` → misses the occurrence, p stays -1, returns 6.

**Multiple occurrences** - two "abc" patterns require updating p each time.
`Input: s = "abcabc"` → `Expected: 14`
⚠️ Bug: setting p only once via `if (p == -1) p = r - 2` → at r = 5 p stays 0, adds 5 instead of 2, returns 17.

**Overflow** - all identical characters with n = 10^5 yields 100000 × 100001 / 2 = 5,000,050,000 > 2^31 − 1.
`Input: s = "aaa...a" (10^5 chars)` → `Expected: 5000050000`
⚠️ Bug: declaring `ans` as `int` → wraps to 705082704.

followUps.q: What if the forbidden pattern is an arbitrary string t of length k instead of "abc"?
followUps.a: Same approach: track p = the start index of the most recent occurrence of t ending at or before r. Checking s[r-k+1..r] == t takes O(k) per step, giving O(nk) time and O(1) space. With a rolling hash or KMP failure function you can reduce the per-step check to O(1) amortized, yielding O(n) time.

followUps.q: What if there are multiple forbidden patterns and a substring is invalid when it contains any of them?
followUps.a: Build an Aho-Corasick automaton over all forbidden patterns. As you scan r left to right, follow transitions and track the deepest match end position p (the maximum start index of any matched pattern ending at or before r). Add r − p at each step. Time is O(n + total pattern length), space is O(total pattern length × alphabet).

followUps.q: What if the string arrives as a stream, one character at a time, and you must report the running count with O(1) memory?
followUps.a: Keep only the last two characters (to detect "abc") and the current p. When a new character arrives at position r, check if the last three form "abc" and update p = r − 2 if so, then add r − p to the running total. This uses O(1) space and O(1) time per character, identical logic to the batch version.
